In the Supreme Court of the United States
NATIONAL REPUBLICAN CONGRESSIONAL COMMITTEE 
AND NATIONAL REPUBLICAN SENATORIAL COMMITTEE,
APPLICANTS,
v.
SHERROD BROWN, JON OSSOFF, ROY COOPER,
AND KRISTEN MCDONALD RIVET,
RESPONDENTS.
EMERGENCY APPLICATION FOR STAY AND ADMINISTRATIVE STAY
PENDING PETITION FOR WRIT OF CERTIORARI
To the Honorable John G. Roberts, Jr.,
Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States and
Circuit Justice for the Fourth Circuit
August 28, 2026
THOMAS R. MCCARTHY
Counsel of Record
DAVID L. ROSENTHAL
CONOR D. WOODFIN
Consovoy McCarthy, PLLC
1600 Wilson Blvd, Ste. 700
Arlington, VA 22209
(703) 243-9423
tom@consovoymccarthy.com
Counsel for NRCC and NRSC

- ii -
PARTIES TO THE PROCEEDING AND RELATED PROCEEDINGS
The parties to the proceeding below are as follows: 
Applicants are the National Republican Congressional Committee and the 
National Republican Senatorial Committee. Applicants were intervenor-respondents in the court of appeals proceedings.
Respondents are Sherrod Brown, Jon Ossoff, Roy Cooper, and Kristen McDonald Rivet. Respondents were applicants in the agency proceedings and petitioners in 
the court of appeals proceedings.
The Federal Communications Commission and the United States of America 
are also Respondents. They were respondents in the agency proceedings and in the 
court of appeals proceedings.
The related proceedings below are:
1. Brown v. Federal Communications Commission, No. 26-1785 (4th Cir.) 
– Judgment entered August 25, 2026;
2. In the Matter of Entitlement to Lowest Unit Charge for Legally Qualified Candidates for Federal Office and All Authorized Committees, DA 
26-300 (Federal Communications Commission) – Proposed order on 
circulation.

- iii -
CORPORATE DISCLOSURE STATEMENT
Per Supreme Court Rule 29, Applicants the National Republican Congressional Committee and the National Republican Senatorial Committee state that they 
have no parent companies or publicly held companies with a 10% or greater ownership interest in them.

- 1 -
TO THE HONORABLE JOHN G. ROBERTS, JR., CHIEF JUSTICE OF THE SUPREME 
COURT OF THE UNITED STATES AND CIRCUIT JUSTICE FOR THE FOURTH CIRCUIT:
In the midst of election season, a divided Fourth Circuit panel just rewrote
longstanding rules about preferential broadcast rates for political ads. At the behest 
of Democratic candidates who said those rules favor their electoral opponents, the 
panel majority blew through two jurisdictional bars to vacate a staff-level public notice that is neither final nor an agency action. The order splits with multiple circuits, 
“restrict[s] political speech in the sensitive period leading up to an election,” App. 90 
(Wilkinson, J., dissenting), and ignores this Court’s recent instruction on agency finality, see Trump v. California, No. 26A124, 609 U.S. __, slip op. at 7-8 (Aug. 24, 2026)
(per curiam). Applicants have budgeted tens of millions of dollars in ad buys under 
these rules. But because of the Fourth Circuit’s decision, broadcast stations are already rescinding those rates. 
The Federal Election Campaign Act amended the Communications Act to afford candidates and committees favorable advertising rates from broadcasting stations during election season, so long as those ads are for candidate “use.” 47 U.S.C. 
§315(b)(1). Settled agency and industry interpretation of that law has long guaranteed those favorable rates to coordinated ad buys between candidates and committees, and to joint fundraising committee ad buys for candidate use. So, for example, 
when “a political party” exercises its First Amendment right to “spend money to produce and place a television advertisement in support of a candidate,” Nat’l Republican Senatorial Comm. v. FEC, 146 S. Ct. 2404, 2415 (2026), the FEC Act guarantees 
it reduced rates at the “lowest unit charge of the station,” 47 U.S.C. §315(b)(1)(A).

- 2 -
In March, the FCC’s Media Bureau issued interpretive guidance in the form of 
a public notice. App. 106-107. That public notice “remind[ed] broadcasters and the 
public” about the Commission’s requirements for political ad buys. App. 106. It reiterated that favorable rates are guaranteed to “authorized committees that engage in 
joint fundraising with legally qualified candidates” and to “advertisements that qualify as coordinated expenditures.” App. 106.
Respondents—Democratic House and Senate candidates—disagree with that 
interpretation. And they say it helps their rivals, because committees like the NRCC 
and NRSC have more money that they spend on ads in tandem with Republican candidates. So they sought to upend the status quo by getting a court to say that only 
candidates are entitled to those favorable rates. In April, Respondents filed an application with the FCC asking the full Commission to review and set aside the Media 
Bureau’s public notice. 
Although the Commission was—and still is—considering that application for 
review, see App. 93-94, Respondents sought review of the Commission’s non-action. 
The Fourth Circuit granted their petition, “seiz[ing] imaginary jurisdiction” to vacate 
the staff-level guidance still awaiting the full Commission’s review. App. 90. (Wilkinson, J., dissenting).
The order is wrong for several reasons, but Applicants focus primarily on the 
jurisdictional bars to review: the Fourth Circuit lacked jurisdiction to review and vacate interpretive guidance that is neither agency action, nor final. The panel’s disregard of its jurisdiction to review a public notice that is not agency action—while an

- 3 -
application for the agency’s review was pending—splits with multiple circuits, “neuter[s] a federal agency,” and “disfavor[s] the place of political parties in our democratic dialogue” on the eve of the election. App. 90.
Accordingly, Applicants request an immediate stay and administrative stay of the Fourth Circuit’s judgment before the statutory rates take 
effect on September 4, 2026.
STATEMENT OF THE CASE
A. In 1971, Congress enacted the Federal Election Campaign Act. In part, that 
law set rules for how broadcasting stations must treat candidates and campaigns 
during election season. Among other things, during the 45 days preceding a primary 
election or 60 days preceding a general election, any charges “for the use of any broadcasting station by any person who is a legally qualified candidate for any public office 
in connection with his campaign … shall not exceed … the lowest unit charge of the 
station for the same class and amount of time for the same period.” 47 U.S.C. 
§315(b)(1)(A). That “lowest unit charge” became known as the LUC rate.
For years, coordinated ad buys and joint fundraising committee ad buys for 
candidate use have received the favorable LUC rate. App. 71 (Wilkinson, J., dissenting). The FCC and the broadcasting industry have long taken that position. Respondents have “profited” from it themselves. App. 71. And the practice continues today: 
broadcasters are providing LUC rates in remaining ongoing primary-election windows, while candidates and parties have already purchased LUC-rate advertising 
flights for the general election season.

- 4 -
Respondents in this case sought to upset that status quo. Seeking a “competitive” advantage over their political rivals, App. 132, Respondents filed an application 
with the FCC asking the Commission to end the practice of giving favorable lowest 
unit rates to coordinated ad buys and joint fundraising committees’ advertisements. 
App. 114. They challenge a public notice issued by the Commission’s Media Bureau 
in March. That public notice “remind[ed] broadcasters and the public about the FCC’s 
lowest unit charge (LUC) requirements.” App. 106. It reiterated that the lowest unit 
rate applies to both “authorized committees, including authorized committees that 
engage in joint fundraising with legally qualified candidates for federal office,” and 
to “advertisements that qualify as coordinated expenditures of political parties and 
legally qualified candidates for federal office.” App. 106. Respondents filed an application for review, asking the full Commission to revisit and set aside that guidance. 
The Commission is still considering that application. See App. 93-98. 
Without waiting for the full Commission to act, Respondents sought review of 
the Commission’s non-action in the Fourth Circuit. The court granted Respondents’ 
request for expedited briefing, allowed the NRCC and NRSC to intervene as circuitcourt respondents, and held oral argument on August 7. App. 23, 25, 28. On August 
17, the Commission filed a Rule 28(j) letter informing the Fourth Circuit that the 
Commission had circulated a draft order on Respondents’ application for review, noting that the proceeding remains nonfinal. App. 93-94. On August 25, the Court issued

- 5 -
its opinion and order granting the petition, denying the Commission’s motion to dismiss, and setting aside “the Public Notice issued by the FCC’s Media Bureau.” App.
51. 
B. On jurisdiction, the majority said it was “confident of [its] jurisdiction to 
review the Public Notice.” App. 31. The circuit courts have jurisdiction over “final 
orders of the Federal Communications Commission.” 28 U.S.C. §2342(1). The majority concluded that the staff-level public notice was “an order ‘of the Commission’” because it “has ‘the same force and effect’ as orders of the Commission.” App. 32-33
(quoting 47 U.S.C. §155(c)(3)). And it concluded the order was “final” for three reasons. First, the majority thought that “an otherwise final order of the Commission …
becomes nonfinal when the order is ‘reviewed as provided in [47 U.S.C. §155(c)(4)].’”
App. 33 (alteration in original). And because the Commission had “begun” its review
of Respondents’ application but had not “completed” that review by the time Respondents filed their Fourth Circuit petition, the order was still “final.” App. 33-34 (citing
47 U.S.C. §155(c)(3), (4)). Second, the majority reasoned that the Commission’s “inaction” on the Respondents’ application had “constructively denied the Application for 
FCC Review and adopted the Public Notice” by implication, rendering it “final.” App.
34. And third, the majority thought that the public notice is “a legislative rule,” not 
an “interpretive rule,” and is thus “necessarily the law of the land and final” despite 
the public notice still pending before the full Commission. App. 36-37.

- 6 -
On the merits, the majority concluded that the Public Notice “unlawfully requires broadcasters to extend the LUC to political parties and joint fundraising committees with non-candidate members.” App. 39. It reasoned that the “statutory text 
is unambiguous,” App. 41, emphasizing that the LUC rate applies “for the use of any 
broadcasting station by any person who is a legally qualified candidate for any public 
office in connection with his campaign,” 47 U.S.C. §315(b)(1)(A) (emphasis added). It 
rejected the argument that “party coordinated expenditures and spending by joint 
fundraising committees with non-candidate members involve ‘use … by’ the candidate.” App. 42. Those expenditures, the majority reasoned, are “the political party’s 
use — not the candidate’s use.” App. 44. Neither do ad buys by joint fundraising committees count as “the candidate’s use,” the majority ruled, even if the joint fundraising 
committee is “designated as the ‘authorized committee’ of a participating candidate.” 
App. 47-48. The panel thus granted the petition for review and “set aside as unlawful 
… the Public Notice issued by the FCC’s Media Bureau.” App. 51.
Judge Wilkinson dissented on all points. He began by criticizing the majority 
for “transgress[ing] its jurisdictional bounds.” App. 61 (Wilkinson, J., dissenting). To 
challenge delegated agency action, an aggrieved party must first “seek agency review 
by filing an ‘application for review’ before the full Commission within 30 days of public notice of a decision by FCC staff.” App. 65 (citing 47 U.S.C. §155(c)(7); 47 C.F.R. 
§1.115(d)). The Commission then “has a mandatory obligation to act on the application.” App. 65 (citing 47 U.S.C. §155(c)(4)). Only after the Commission passes on the 
application may an aggrieved party file a “petition for review” in federal court. 47

- 7 -
U.S.C. §155(c)(7). And judicial review of the Commission’s decision begins by filing “a 
petition” for review in the appropriate federal court “within 60 days after” the entry 
of a “final order.” 28 U.S.C. §2344. Under these “straightforward” statutes, “[j]udicial 
review is unavailable until the FCC renders a final order.” App. 65. And as Judge 
Wilkinson pointed out, “[t]here is no final order here because the full Commission is 
still formulating its final decision.” App. 65.
Judge Wilkinson rejected the majority’s holding “that merely filing an application for review provides this court with jurisdiction.” App. 66. That interpretation 
“would demand an audacious act of judicial overreach,” and it “disrespects the value 
of agency finality.” App. 66. Judge Wilkinson also rejected the majority’s constructivedenial holding, which “tells the FCC that, moving forward, our court will ignore its 
internal review process unless it renders a decision in two months or less.” App. 71.
He thus criticized the majority for running “roughshod over Congress’s command that 
the agency ‘pass upon’ and ‘dispose of’ petitioners’ application for review.” App. 71
(cleaned up) (quoting 47 U.S.C. §§155(c)(4), (7)).
On the merits, Judge Wilkinson rejected the majority’s strict, narrow reading 
of candidate “use” of a broadcasting station. App. 74-75. He pointed out that “a candidate could ‘use’ a broadcasting station” in many ways. App. 74. And a candidate 
plausibly “uses” a broadcasting station if, for example, an ad “showcases an ordinary 
candidate appearance or blurb,” even if a joint fundraising committee paid for the ad 
space. App. 75-76. The majority’s “narrow” interpretation of “use” “distorts that term 
in a way especially unsuited to the campaign environment.” App. 78.

- 8 -
Moreover, any ambiguity, Judge Wilkinson reasoned, is resolved by the First 
Amendment, which prohibits “using the benefit to candidates to deny comparable 
speech-enhancing benefits to closely coordinating entities.” App. 80. After this Court’s 
decision in NRSC v. FEC, it is “doubt[ful]” that “the First Amendment tolerates 
FECA’s indirect strike against party-coordinated speech any more than it sanctions 
direct limits on the speech of the candidate himself.” App. 87. The majority’s decision 
is “at odds” with that precedent. App. 89.
The day after the Fourth Circuit issued its opinion, Applicants moved for an 
emergency stay. App. 5. Although Judge Wilkinson would have granted the stay, the 
panel majority denied that motion on August 27 and sua sponte expedited issuance 
of the mandate to take effect that day. App. 2, 4. Applicants then moved for a stay in 
this Court.
ARGUMENT
This Court will stay a circuit court’s order if there is “(1) a reasonable probability that four Justices will consider the issue sufficiently meritorious to grant certiorari; (2) a fair prospect that a majority of the Court will vote to reverse the judgment 
below; and (3) a likelihood that irreparable harm will result from the denial of a stay.” 
Hollingsworth v. Perry, 558 U.S. 183, 190 (2010) (per curiam). “In close cases the 
Circuit Justice or the Court will balance the equities and weigh the relative harms to 
the applicant and to the respondent.” Id. Applicants satisfy those standards.

- 9 -
I. There is a reasonable probability that four Justices would vote to 
grant review and a fair prospect that this Court would reverse.
The Fourth Circuit’s decision to review a staff-level guidance document awaiting full Commission review is both cert-worthy and ripe for reversal. The Fourth Circuit “seize[d] imaginary jurisdiction” by vacating an agency’s non-action and disregarding Congress’s requirement that the Commission must first resolve Respondents’
application for review. App. 90 (Wilkinson, J., dissenting). The court’s decision blows 
past two jurisdictional bars and splits from its sister circuits in two ways. 
First, the opinion mistakes staff interpretive guidance for final agency action—
splitting with the D.C. Circuit holding that public notice is not agency action. Second, 
the opinion ignores Congress’s requirement that the Commission resolve Respondents’ application for review before Respondents can seek judicial review—splitting 
from longstanding precedents from three circuits. These missteps “make it reasonably probable that the Court will grant certiorari to resolve the split” on these jurisdictional issues. Maryland v. King, 567 U.S. 1301, 1303 (2012) (Roberts, C.J., in 
chambers). And “given the considered analysis of courts on the other side of the split, 
there is a fair prospect that this Court will reverse the decision below.” Id.
A. The staff-level public notice is not “agency action.”
The Court’s jurisdiction under the Hobbs Act reaches only “final orders of the 
Federal Communications Commission.” 28 U.S.C. §2342(1); 47 U.S.C. §402(a). A final 
order under the Hobbs Act is “analytically identical” to final agency action under the 
Administrative Procedure Act. US W. Commc’ns v. Hamilton, 224 F.3d 1049, 1055 
(9th Cir. 2000). As such, agency action must “be one by which rights or obligations

- 10 -
have been determined, or from which legal consequences will flow.” Bennett v. Spear, 
520 U.S. 154, 177-78 (1997) (cleaned up). Yet the Fourth Circuit held that “the Public 
Notice is, and always has been, a ‘final’ order” because the Media Bureau acted under 
delegated authority. App. 33. 
The majority’s holding ignores Bennett. The Media Bureau’s public notice is at 
most an interpretive guidance document restating the FCC’s longstanding position 
regarding LUC rates. Those sorts of “[i]nterpretive rules … do not have the force and 
effect of law.” Shalala v. Guernsey Mem’l Hosp., 514 U.S. 87, 99 (1995). So they don’t 
qualify for judicial review. See Am. Tort Reform Ass'n v. OSHA, 738 F.3d 387, 395 
(D.C. Cir. 2013) (an agency’s “interpretative rules or statements of policy” are not 
subject to judicial review under the APA). Until the Commission applies that interpretive rule in an enforcement action, the agency’s “decisionmaking process” remains 
ongoing and no “legal consequences will flow” from the guidance document. Bennett, 
520 U.S. at 177-78. The public notice “imposes no legal requirements” on Respondents, and any application of the policy to them or anyone else is “dependent on ‘contingent future events that may not occur as anticipated, or indeed may not occur at 
all.’” Trump v. California, slip op. at 7-8 (quoting Trump v. New York, 592 U.S. 125, 
131 (2020)).
The D.C. Circuit’s rule is right. An FCC bureau order issued under delegated 
authority “is not an order of the Commission,” and “without a final order from the 
Commission” courts lack jurisdiction. NTCH, Inc. v. FCC, 877 F.3d 408, 409-10 (D.C. 
Cir. 2017). “When Congress says ‘the Commission,’ it means the Commission,” not

- 11 -
“delegated subdivisions of the Commission.” Id. at 413. The D.C. Circuit is correct
because the FCC’s application for review is “designed to ensure that if a delegated 
authority … renders a decision, the Commission itself has the opportunity to review 
the decision before this Court considers it.” Id. at 413-14 (quoting Environmentel, 
LLC v. FCC, 661 F.3d 80, 83 (D.C. Cir. 2011)). In doing so, Congress “prevent[ed] a 
party from appealing directly to [the circuit court] from a decision made by a delegated authority.” Environmentel, 661 F.3d at 84. The Fourth Circuit’s decision deeming the Media Bureau’s guidance to be agency action is wrong and splits with the D.C. 
Circuit. This Court would likely reverse. 
B. The public notice is not a “final” agency action.
Even if the public notice were an “agency action,” it’s far from a “final” agency 
action. The Fourth Circuit’s contrary decision runs headlong into well-reasoned precedents of at least three circuits on finality. The Communications Act makes “filing” 
an application for review with the full Commission “a condition precedent to judicial 
review” of a staff-decision taken pursuant to delegated authority—e.g., Media Bureau 
decisions. 47 U.S.C. §155(c)(1), (7). Congress specified in the very next sentence that 
“[t]he time within which a petition for review [in court] shall be computed from the 
date upon which public notice is given of orders disposing of all applications for review” before the Commission.” Id. §155(c)(7) (emphasis added); see also United States 
v. Morton, 467 U.S. 822, 828 (1984) (“We do not … construe statutory phrases in isolation; we read statutes as a whole”). The Hobbs Act then permits parties aggrieved 
by a final order of the Commission to “file a petition to review the order” in court 
“within 60 days after its entry.” 28 U.S.C. §§2342(1), 2344; 47 U.S.C. §402(a).

- 12 -
So parties who seek to challenge an action taken pursuant to delegated authority “must proceed in two steps.” App. 63 (Wilkinson, J., dissenting). First, a party 
must file an “application for review” of the staff decision before the full Commission. 
47 U.S.C. §155(c)(7). Second, within 60 days after the Commission issues a final order 
disposing of all applications for review, a party may file a “petition for review” in 
federal court. Id. “The obligation to file within that sixty-day window” imposed by the 
Hobbs Act is “jurisdictional in nature, and may not be enlarged or altered by the 
courts, at least absent exceptional circumstances.” Bhd. of Locomotive Eng’rs & 
Trainmen v. Fed. R.R. Admin., 972 F.3d 83, 103 (D.C. Cir. 2020) (cleaned up).
As Judge Wilkinson reasoned, the “jurisdictional question at hand is thus a 
straightforward matter of statutory interpretation.” App. 64. “Judicial review is unavailable until the FCC renders a final order.” App. 64. But “because the full Commission is still formulating its final decision” on Respondents’ application for review of 
the public notice, no final order exists here. App. 64. The Fourth Circuit’s decision to 
reach the merits of a petition for review “before the Commission has even ‘dispos[ed] 
of all applications for review’ pending before it impermissibly enlarges the filing window.” App. 65 (quoting 47 U.S.C. §155(c)(7)). 
Congress’s jurisdictional rule would mean nothing if the Commission does not 
“need to resolve the application prior to judicial review.” App. 64 (Wilkinson, J., dissenting). As then-Judge Scalia explained, “[i]f the intent were to establish a filing 
deadline rather than a filing window, it would more naturally have been phrased ‘no 
later than 60 days after … entry’ rather than ‘within 60 days after … entry.’” W.

- 13 -
Union Tel. Co. v. FCC, 773 F.2d 375, 377 (D.C. Cir. 1985) (declining to exercise jurisdiction over a premature appeal of an FCC order). Because the statute establishes a 
filing window—not merely a deadline—that has not yet opened here, see App. 93-98—
the panel opinion’s jurisdictional analysis contravenes Congress’s statutory requirement. 
The Fourth Circuit stands alone, splitting from every other circuit that has 
decided this jurisdictional question. As Judge Wilkinson recognized, App. 67, the 
Third, Eleventh, and D.C. Circuits have all ruled that the Hobbs Act requires the 
Commission to rule on an application for review before a challenge may proceed in 
court. Ala. Power Co. v. FCC, 311 F.3d 1357, 1366 (11th Cir. 2002) (“[T]he Commission must in some way act on the application for review before a party may petition 
a court of appeals for review.”); accord Council Tree Commc’ns v. FCC, 503 F.3d 284, 
287 (3d Cir. 2007); Ga. Power Co. v. Teleport Commc’ns Atlanta, 346 F.3d 1047, 1050 
(11th Cir. 2003); Int’l Telecard Ass’n v. FCC, 166 F.3d 387, 387-88 (D.C. Cir. 1999); 
see also Sierra Club v. NRC, 825 F.2d 1356, 1359 (9th Cir. 1987). Yet the Fourth 
Circuit allowed Respondents to side-step this Hobbs Act requirement by reaching the 
merits of an “incurably premature” petition. TeleSTAR, Inc. v. FCC, 888 F.2d 132, 
134 (D.C. Cir. 1989); Council Tree Commc’ns, 503 F.3d at 287. This mistake warrants
a stay because courts “may not enlarge [their] jurisdiction on a whim.” App. 64 (Wilkinson, J., dissenting). 
The Fourth Circuit sought to avoid this requirement by concluding that the 
Commission “constructively denied” Respondents’ application for review. App. 34-35.

- 14 -
But its opinion would be the first in the Communications Act’s 92-year history to find 
constructive denial. App. 16. Agency inaction—especially for such a short period of 
time—does not transform non-final guidance into final action. And inaction is not the 
same as a denial, particularly in the regulatory review process. See Bennett, 520 U.S.
at 177-78; FTC v. Standard Oil Co. of Cal., 449 U.S. 232, 241-43 (1980). Even if 
agency inaction over a long period of time could warrant a mandamus remedy, this 
case is nowhere near such extraordinary relief (which is why Respondents never 
sought mandamus). App. 69-70 (Wilkinson, J., dissenting). The Fourth Circuit 
usurped the Commission’s opportunity to complete the first pass upon the application. 47 U.S.C. §155(c)(4). As a result, “[c]ountless future FCC staff decisions are vulnerable to hasty appeal” in the Fourth Circuit, “short-circuiting the Commission’s 
internal review process.” App. 70. A stay is warranted to prevent a jurisdictional error 
that splits from every other circuit to have addressed this finality requirement.
C. The Fourth Circuit myopically construed a candidate’s “use” of 
an ad to mean the candidate’s “exclusive funding” of the ad.
The jurisdictional errors alone justify a stay and “should end [the] inquiry.”
App. 89 (Wilkinson, J., dissenting). But the Fourth Circuit erred on the merits, too. 
Congress empowered the FCC to regulate broadcasters’ treatment of political advertising based on candidate “use.” In particular, broadcasters must offer “a legally qualified candidate” for a federal office “and any authorized committee of the candidate” 
the lowest unit charge for “use of any broadcasting station” in the runup to an election. 47 U.S.C. §315(b)(1). In no uncertain terms, the touchstone for applying the lowest unit charge requirement is candidate “use.”

- 15 -
The Fourth Circuit employed a “very narrow, literal view of ‘use’” to deny LUC 
rates to candidate-party coordinated and joint fundraising committee ads because the 
candidate doesn’t pay for those ads. App. 74 (Wilkinson, J., dissenting). As Judge 
Wilkinson explained, “‘use’ cannot be quite so narrow” in this statute. App. 74. Indeed, a candidate might “use” a broadcasting station by appearing in an advertisement authorized by the candidate. 47 C.F.R. §73.1942(a)-(b) (FCC implementing regulation). The touchstone of “use” has nothing to do with who foots the bill—be it the 
candidate personally, the principal campaign committee, a party committee, or some 
combination of those. See App. 75. 
Context confirms that the “use” means “use,” not “payment.” The Communications Act’s text expressly affords the lowest unit charge to “the candidate (and any authorized committee of the candidate).” 47 U.S.C. §315(b)(2)(A) (emphasis added). So 
the statute entitles more than simply the candidate and the principal campaign committee to the LUC, but “any” authorized committee. “Read naturally, the word ‘any’
has an expansive meaning, that is, ‘one or some indiscriminately of whatever kind.’”
United States v. Gonzales, 520 U.S. 1, 5 (1997) (quoting Webster’s Third New International Dictionary 97 (1976)). As Judge Wilkinson observed, “any” authorized committee of the candidate includes joint fundraising committees. App. 75 (citing 52 
U.S.C. §30102(e)(3)(A)(ii)). The law removes any doubt by permitting candidates to 
designate a joint fundraising committee “as an authorized committee” under the FEC
Act. 52 U.S.C. §30102(e)(3)(A)(ii). “The text of the Communications Act,” according to 
Judge Wilkinson, “favor[s]” Applicants’ view on the merits as well. App. 74.

- 16 -
As Judge Wilkinson went on to explain, to the extent any doubt remained about 
how to interpret the statute, the First Amendment resolves it in Applicants’ favor. 
App. 79-89. Coordination between candidates and parties “has formed the essence of 
our Nation’s party system of government” since the Founding. NRSC, 146 S. Ct. at 
2416. Restricting that political coordination “abridge[s] political parties’ freedom of 
speech.” Id. at 2412. So laws that inhibit political-party coordination, such as “political-party coordinated-expenditure limits,” “violate the First Amendment.” Id. at 
2428. The Fourth Circuit’s order inhibits political-party coordination by interpreting 
the Communications Act in a manner that “favors some … modes of candidate speech 
while disfavoring others.” App. 81 (Wilkinson, J., dissenting). Congress generally 
“may not deny a benefit to a person on a basis that infringes his constitutionally protected freedom of speech even if he has no entitlement to that benefit.” Agency for 
Int’l Dev. v. All. for Open Soc’y Int’l, 570 U.S. 205, 214 (2013) (cleaned up). The Fourth 
Circuit’s application of “discriminatory LUC rules present[s] an indirect version” of 
coordinated-expenditure limits “by penalizing candidates for favoring collaborative 
speech over solo self-promotion.” App. 87 (Wilkinson, J., dissenting). Even looking 
past the irredeemable jurisdictional errors, Applicants are likely to prevail on the 
merits. 
II. The remaining factors warrant a stay.
The remaining factors—irreparable harm, the balance of equities, and the public interest—each favor a stay. Hollingsworth, 558 U.S. at 190.

- 17 -
A. Applicants will be irreparably harmed without a stay.
Applicants will suffer irreparable harm if the Fourth Circuit’s order remains 
in effect on September 4. On that date, Applicants should receive statutorily favored 
LUC rates on campaign ads nationwide. But if the Fourth Circuit’s order remains in 
effect, they won’t. Candidates and committees depend on “coordinated expenditures” 
to win elections. NRSC, 146 S. Ct. at 2416. “[P]arty-coordinated ads received LUC 
rates in prior election cycles,” App. 71 (Wilkinson, J., dissenting), allowing parties 
and candidates to collaborate effectively on broadcasted ads. Each day that passes 
under the Fourth Circuit’s order will deprive Applicants of that “statutorily protected 
interest,” setting them up to “compete for office in contests” under practices previously allowed “under FEC rules.” Shays v. FEC, 414 F.3d 76, 85 (D.C. Cir. 2005). 
“Departures from [those] preordained rules cause them particularized and concrete 
harm.” Bost v. Ill. State Bd. of Elections, 607 U.S. 71, 79 (2026). Through their coordinated committees, Applicants have budgeted tens of millions of dollars in ad buys 
at the LUC rates under these rules. But because of the Fourth Circuit’s decision, 
broadcast stations in some States have already rescinded those rates. And because 
Applicants can’t get back their spent money or their lost “opportunities to persuade 
the electorate,” those harms are irreparable. Shays, 414 F.3d at 85. 
In addition to inflicting these harms on Applicants at this critical juncture during election season, the order impairs Applicants’ First Amendment rights. See supra
Section I.C. The Fourth Circuit’s application of “discriminatory LUC rules” infringes 
Applicants’ right to speak and coordinate freely “by penalizing candidates for favoring 
collaborative speech over solo self-promotion.” App. 87 (Wilkinson, J., dissenting).

- 18 -
That restriction of First Amendment rights “unquestionably constitutes irreparable 
injury.” Elrod v. Burns, 427 U.S. 347, 373 (1976). 
Compounding these injuries, the Fourth Circuit changed the rules on the eve

KING, Circuit Judge:
This time-sensitive matter concerns who is entitled to particularly favorable rates 
— known as the “lowest unit charge,” or “LUC” — for broadcast campaign advertisements 
in the run-up to elections. The statutory LUC requirement provides that during the 45-day 
period preceding a primary election and the 60-day period preceding a general election, 
“[t]he charges made for the use of any broadcasting station by any person who is a legally 
qualified candidate for any public office in connection with his campaign” must be at “the 
lowest unit charge of the station for the same class and amount of time for the same period.” 
See 47 U.S.C. § 315(b)(1)(A).
There is no question that candidates are entitled to the LUC. But it is disputed 
whether political parties and joint fundraising committees with non-candidate members
can also be entitled to the LUC. The Federal Communications Commission (the “FCC,” 
or the “Commission”) has asserted that they can, saying so in a “Public Notice” issued by 
the FCC’s Media Bureau on March 30, 2026. 
The Petition for Review before us challenges the Public Notice, which takes effect 
on September 4, 2026, for the impending November general election. The four petitioners, 
all Democrats, are U.S. House of Representatives candidate Kristen McDonald Rivet of 
Michigan and U.S. Senate candidates Sherrod Brown of Ohio, Jon Ossoff of Georgia, and 
Roy Cooper of North Carolina (collectively, the “Federal Candidates”). Their contention 
is that the Public Notice contravenes the plain language of the LUC requirement and 
pertinent campaign finance statutes. In the Federal Candidates’ words, the Public Notice 
“unlawfully dilutes [their] and other candidates’ statutory right to buy advertising time at

I. INTRODUCTION
1. In this Order on Reconsideration, we consider a petition from the Television Bureau of 
Advertising, Inc. (TVB) for reconsideration of the Media Bureau’s March 2026 public notice reminding 
broadcasters and the public about the FCC’s “lowest unit charge” (LUC) requirements.1 For the reasons 
stated below, we dismiss TVB’s request for reconsideration.2 
2. First, TVB argues that the Bureau’s Public Notice broke new substantive ground, and 
their Petition thus seeks reconsideration of what they contend is a new and final agency action. As 
explained below, however, that premise is incorrect. The Public Notice merely reminds the public, going 
into an election season, of the agency’s longstanding and previous decisions regarding the scope of LUC 
obligations. It simply collects in one place prior FCC orders and other relevant authority so that a wide 
range of stakeholders can be aware of existing law. Such a reminder is not a decision or action that can 
be challenged through a petition for reconsideration. 
3. Second, and given the above, insofar as TVB’s Petition takes issue with prior agency 
guidance, the time for challenging that prior guidance has passed.3 Moreover, there is nothing in the 
Public Notice that reopened those issues or underlying guidance sufficient to provide TVB with a right to 
challenge them through a petition for reconsideration of the Public Notice. Likewise, insofar as TVB 
appears to take issue with the longstanding definition of “authorized committee,” which comes from 52 
U.S.C. §§ 30101-30102, they are seeking the wrong type of relief in the wrong forum. Changing that 
definition is an issue for Congress, or the Federal Election Commission (FEC) through its implementing 
rules, to decide. 
4. Third, we note that existing industry practice comports with the FCC’s existing 
interpretations of the LUC requirements. This further confirms that the Public Notice broke no new 
ground; it did not change the status quo. As always, if there are particular instances in which a party

II. BACKGROUND
5. Under section 315(b) of the Communications Act, during the period immediately 
preceding an election, any “use” of broadcast airtime for campaign advertisements “by any person who is 
a legally qualified candidate for any public office” must receive the “lowest unit charge” that the station 
offers for that airtime.5 The statute directs the Commission to “prescribe appropriate rules and regulations 
to carry out” that requirement.6 The Commission has accordingly implemented section 315(b) of the Act 
in section 73.1942 of its rules,7 and in various other rules and orders.8
6. Neither section 315 of the Act nor section 73.1942 of the Commission’s rules specifies 
what “use” of broadcast airtime “by” a candidate entails. But as TVB repeatedly acknowledges, the 
Commission and industry have long recognized the Commission that the LUC entitlement extends to both 
candidates and their principal campaign committees.9 And previous Media Bureau guidance, in response 
to informal inquiries from regulated parties, has established candidate-party coordinated advertisements 
as eligible for the LUC rate.
7. In the Public Notice, the Bureau broke no new ground. Rather, consistent with the 
longstanding, undisputed recognition that principal campaign committees are eligible for the LUC, and 
with section 315(b)(2)(F) of the Act, the Bureau explained that “[t]o determine what qualifies as an 
authorized committee,” the Commission is bound by the meaning given that term by the Federal Election 
Campaign Act (FECA).10 Accordingly, the Bureau stated that “joint fundraising committee[s]”—
committees authorized to raise funds jointly with other candidates, committees, or organizations—are 
entitled to the LUC rate when purchasing airtime for use by a participating candidate.11
8. In addition, the Public Notice includes a reminder that “candidate-party coordinated ads,” 
in which a candidate uses airtime jointly with his or her political party’s national or state committee to 
broadcast “advertisements that qualify as coordinated expenditures of political parties and legally 
qualified candidates for federal office,” are entitled to the LUC.12

parties, [Political Action Committees], and other participants in the political advertising marketplace all 
understood, under the Act and FCC rules, that only a candidate and their singular designated principal 
campaign committee were entitled to the LUC.”13 On this premise, TVB contends that the Public Notice

III. DISCUSSION
10. The central premise of TVB’s Petition—that the Public Notice announces “new political 
broadcasting requirements” that would “upend” existing practice15—is wrong many times over. 
11. As an initial matter, the Public Notice does not adopt any new rules or requirements. 
Instead, it simply “remind[s] broadcasters and the public” about the FCC’s existing LUC requirements 
and “restate[s] previous Media Bureau guidance,” to ensure that broadcasters and the public are aware, 
going into an election season, of how the FCC has previously interpreted the LUC requirements.16 The 
FCC routinely provides these types of reminders. Therefore, we dismiss the Petition because the Public 
Notice is not the type of action that can be challenged through a petition for reconsideration. 
12. TVB’s real issue appears to be with past agency guidance. But the time for filing 
petitions for reconsideration or otherwise challenging earlier guidance has long since passed. Moreover, 
there is nothing in the Public Notice that reopens or otherwise creates a new opportunity to challenge the 
agency’s prior determinations. TVB’s Petition is thus an untimely attempt to challenge prior agency 
actions.17 
13. In addition, the underlying LUC requirements established in law and in prior FCC 
guidance comport with existing industry practice. This confirms that the Public Notice broke no new 
ground, but merely summarized the status quo. 
14. Candidate-party coordinated ads. The Public Notice’s discussion of candidate-party 
coordinated ads takes no new action and breaks no new ground, but merely “restate[s] previous Media

prevailing practice among broadcasters has been to make the LUC available for party-coordinated ads for

15. Joint Fundraising Committees. The Public Notice also correctly recognizes that the

SUMMARY
In 1971, to address candidates’ ballooning campaign costs, Congress required broadcast 
stations to provide special low rates—known as “lowest unit charge”—to candidates in the run-up 
to elections. The plain text of the resulting statute, codified at Section 315(b) of the 
Communications Act, reflects this limited purpose—it entitles only “candidates” to the special 
rates. 47 U.S.C. § 315(b)(1). But the Media Bureau recently issued guidance purporting to require 
broadcast stations to offer lowest unit charge to advertising purchased by two categories of noncandidate political committees: (1) party committees engaged in coordinated expenditures and (2) 
“Joint Fundraising Committees” (JFCs) with candidate and non-candidate committee members. 
That guidance directly conflicts with the plain text of the Communications Act and the 
Commission should set it aside, making clear that only candidates and candidate committees are 
entitled to lowest unit charge. 
Advertisements by party committees are not entitled to lowest unit charge because they are 
not “use” of a broadcasting station “by . . . a legally qualified candidate,” id., even if they are 
“coordinated” with a candidate. The Federal Election Campaign Act (FECA) distinguishes 
between (1) party committee contributions to candidate committees for the candidate’s own use, 
see 52 U.S.C. § 30116(a)(1)(A), (h), and (2) party committee coordinated expenditures, which 
must be made directly by the party committee, see id. § 30116(d). The latter are “use” by a party 
committee, not by a candidate, because they are required to be the party committee’s 
expenditures—if they were the candidate’s use, they would be unlawful contributions to the 
candidate’s committee. 
Advertisements by JFCs with candidate and non-candidate members are also not entitled 
to lowest unit charge because, by law, much of the cost of those advertisements is borne by noncandidate members who are not entitled to lowest unit charge. See 11 C.F.R. § 102.17(c)(7). The

BACKGROUND
I. Statutory and regulatory framework
A. The “lowest unit charge” entitlement
Section 315(b)(1) of the Communications Act of 1934 entitles “legally qualified 
candidate[s] for any public office” who “use . . . any broadcasting station” shortly before their 
elections to do so at “the lowest unit charge of the station for the same class and amount of time 
for the same period.” 47 U.S.C. § 315(b)(1). This valuable entitlement takes effect 45 days before 
the candidate’s primary election or runoff and 60 days before the candidate’s general election. Id.
